title_en: Hong Kong Green Valley Investment Company v. Canada Green Valley (International) Investment Company, et al. — equity dispute
keywords_en: Civil; Equity dispute; Second instance; Supreme People's Court; Shanghai; Hong Kong Special Administrative Region; Legal person; Foreign-invested enterprise; Law on Sino-Foreign Equity Joint Ventures; Civil Procedure Law; Effectiveness of approval for equity change; Boundary between civil litigation and administrative litigation; Determination of shareholder identity; Dismissal of claims; Sino-foreign equity joint venture; Equity transfer; Company name change; Approval procedure; Administrative litigation; Equity disputes involving investment companies, etc.
full_text_en:
Hong Kong Green Valley Investment Company v. Canada Green Valley (International) Investment Company et al.

— Dispute over Equity

[Ruling Summary]

In accordance with the provisions of the Law of the People's Republic of China on Sino-Foreign Equity Joint Ventures, any change in the equity of a Sino-foreign equity joint venture must be submitted to the competent authority for examination and approval, and the status of the shareholders shall be determined based on the result of such examination and approval. If a party considers an equity change inappropriate and seeks to alter the examination and approval result, such dispute shall be resolved through administrative litigation. If a party files a civil lawsuit requesting the People's Court to modify its equity in a Sino-foreign equity joint venture, the case shall be handled in accordance with Article 111(1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China.

Civil Ruling of the Supreme People's Court

(2002) Min Si Zhong Zi No. 14

Appellant (Defendant at First Instance): Green Valley (International) Investment & Management Ltd. Domicile: #3 Willowheights Court, Willowdale, Ontario, Canada.

Legal Representative: Hao Xiaoying, Chairman of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Liu Zhihong, lawyer at Beijing Shanggong Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Yu Yunhe, lawyer at Shanghai Guangting Law Firm.

Respondent (Plaintiff at First Instance): Green Valley Investment Limited. Domicile: Room 1703, Nan Dao Commercial Building, 359-361 Queen's Road Central, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, People's Republic of China.

Legal Representative: Huang Guangming, Chairman of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Chen Minghao, lawyer at Shanghai Mingli Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Shen Zhigeng, lawyer at Beijing Zongheng Law Firm.

Defendant at First Instance: Shanghai Xinda Industrial General Company. Domicile: No. 431 Hami Road, Shanghai, People's Republic of China.

Legal Representative: Wang Xiangyun, Chairman of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Gao Ronghua, lawyer at Shanghai Xinhong Law Firm.

Defendant at First Instance: Hao Xiaoying, male, born July 4, 1949, residing at Flat 6, 1st Floor, 15 Plantation Road, The Peak, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.

Agent ad litem: Liu Zhihong, lawyer at Beijing Shanggong Law Firm.

The appellant, Green Valley (International) Investment & Management Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Canada Green Valley Company), filed an appeal with this Court against the civil judgment (1998) Hu Gao Min Chu Zi No. 10 rendered by the Shanghai High People's Court in the dispute over equity with the respondent, Green Valley Investment Limited (hereinafter referred to as Hong Kong Green Valley Company), and the defendants at first instance, Shanghai Xinda Industrial General Company (hereinafter referred to as Xinda Company) and Hao Xiaoying. This Court formed a collegial panel in accordance with the law, with Judge Wang Yun as presiding judge, and acting judges Chen Jizhong and Gao Xiaoli participating in the deliberation. The case has now been concluded.

The facts found by the court of first instance are as follows: On March 20, 1987, the Sino-foreign equity joint venture Shanghai Holiday Villa Co., Ltd. was established with a registered capital of US$10 million, of which the Chinese party, Shanghai Huashen Cultural and Entertainment Service Company, contributed US$2 million, and the foreign party, Canada Yingming Development Company (hereinafter referred to as Canada Yingming Company), contributed US$8 million. As the foreign party's capital was not fully contributed, on September 5, 1990, the capital contribution ratio of Shanghai Holiday Villa Co., Ltd. was changed, with the Chinese party contributing US$7.5 million and the foreign party contributing US$2.5 million. On the same day, Shanghai Huashen Cultural and Entertainment Service Company and Hong Kong Kaiyi Industrial Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Hong Kong Kaiyi Company) entered into an Equity Transfer Agreement, stipulating that Hong Kong Kaiyi Company would purchase 55% (US$5.5 million) of the shares of Shanghai Huashen Cultural and Entertainment Service Company in Shanghai Holiday Villa Co., Ltd. This equity transfer was approved by a resolution of the board of directors of Shanghai Holiday Villa Co., Ltd. On September 15 of the same year, the joint venture entities and capital contribution ratios of Shanghai Holiday Villa Co., Ltd. were changed, with the Chinese party Shanghai Huashen Entertainment Service Company contributing US$2 million, the foreign party Canada Yingming Company contributing US$2.5 million, and the foreign party Hong Kong Kaiyi Company contributing US$5.5 million. On February 12, 1991, Shanghai Holiday Villa Co., Ltd. underwent a name change registration with the administrative authorities for industry and commerce and was renamed Shanghai Green Valley Villa Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Shanghai Green Valley Company).

On February 16, 1991, Hong Kong Kaiyi Company sent a letter to the board of directors of Shanghai Green Valley Company, stating: "Due to the development of Hong Kong Kaiyi Company's business and the reform of its corporate structure, the name of Hong Kong Kaiyi Company, which was originally registered and used in Shanghai Green Valley Company, is now changed to Hong Kong Green Valley Company. Henceforth, all creditor's rights and debts of the former Hong Kong Kaiyi Company in Shanghai Green Valley Company shall be fully assumed by Hong Kong Green Valley Company. Please confirm in the agreement." On July 18 of the same year, Hong Kong Green Valley Company was registered and established at the Hong Kong Companies Registry. On January 5, 1992, Hong Kong Green Valley Company and Hong Kong Kaiyi Company entered into an Equity Transfer Agreement, stipulating that all shares of Hong Kong Kaiyi Company in Shanghai Green Valley Company (US$5.5 million, accounting for 55%) would be transferred to Hong Kong Green Valley Company, and entrusted Lu Jiadong and Huang Yaolin to handle the relevant legal procedures. On the same day, Hong Kong Kaiyi Company sent a letter to Shanghai Green Valley Company, stating: "Due to the overall adjustment of our company's business in Hong Kong, after study by the board of directors, it is decided to change the company name to Hong Kong Green Valley Company. Please assist in handling the relevant legal procedures such as replacing the approval certificate and industrial and commercial registration." On March 4 of the same year, the Shanghai Foreign Investment Work Committee issued Hu Wai Zi Wei Xie Zi (92) No. 158, "Reply on the Name Change of the Hong Kong Investor of Shanghai Green Valley Company," stating: "Since the Hong Kong investor of Shanghai Green Valley Company — Hong Kong Kaiyi Company — has changed its name to Hong Kong Green Valley Company, it is agreed to make corresponding amendments to the relevant clauses of the contract and articles of association of Shanghai Green Valley Company." On March 23 of the same year, the Shanghai Municipal People's Government issued to Shanghai Green Valley Company the "Approval Certificate for Sino-Foreign Equity Joint Ventures of the People's Republic of China," Wai Jing Mao Hu Zi Zi (1987) No. 005, listing the joint venture parties as Shanghai Huashen Cultural and Entertainment Service Company, Canada Yingming Company, and Hong Kong Green Valley Company.

On April 6, 1992, a meeting attended by all directors of Hong Kong Green Valley Company passed a resolution to redistribute the shares of Hong Kong Green Valley Company, with Huang Yaolin, Huang Guangming, Liu Jianguo, Hao Xiaoying, and Lu Jiadong each holding 20%.

On September 16, 1995, Canada Green Valley Company and Hao Xiaoying issued a "Statement on the Renaming of Hong Kong Green Valley Company to Canada Green Valley Company," stating: "The third-party investor of Shanghai Green Valley Company is Hong Kong Green Valley Company. Now, because the company has moved to Canada and is registered in Canada, the former Hong Kong Green Valley Company is renamed Canada Green Valley Company. The legal representative and chairman have not changed, and the equity of the third-party investor of Shanghai Green Valley Company remains unchanged." On October 11 of the same year, the Changning District People's Government of Shanghai issued Chang Fu Wai Jing Fa (1995) No. 225, "Reply on Agreeing to the Equity Transfer of Shanghai Green Valley Company," stating: "1. Agree that all equity of the original investor, Party A Shanghai Huashen Cultural and Entertainment Service Company, in Shanghai Green Valley Company shall be transferred to Xinda Company; 2. Agree that the original third-party investor, Hong Kong Green Valley Company, due to its reincorporation in Canada, shall be changed to Canada Green Valley Company; 3. After the above adjustments, the three investing parties of Shanghai Green Valley Company shall be: Party A Xinda Company (Chinese party), Party B Canada Yingming Company, and Party C Canada Green Valley Company. The investment ratios and profit distribution ratios of all parties remain unchanged, and corresponding amendments shall be made to the relevant sections of the original company contract and articles of association." On October 24 of the same year, Shanghai Green Valley Company applied for change of registration with the Shanghai Administration for Industry and Commerce. On November 23 of the same year, the Shanghai Administration for Industry and Commerce approved the change of registration. On May 25, 1998, the Shanghai Municipal People's Government issued to Shanghai Green Valley Company the "Foreign Investment Enterprise Approval Certificate of the People's Republic of China," Wai Jing Mao Hu He Zi Zi (1997) No. 0005, listing the investors of the joint venture as Xinda Company, Canada Yingming Company, and Canada Green Valley Company.

On May 2, 1998, Hong Kong Green Valley Company held an extraordinary general meeting in Hong Kong. Huang Guangming and Huang Yaolin attended, with Huang Yaolin also representing Liu Xinran. Hao Xiaoying and Lu Jiadong were absent. The meeting resolved to authorize two lawyers from Shanghai Mingli Law Firm to act as agents in the dispute arising from the Shanghai Green Valley Company project in which the company invested, and to authorize Huang Guangming and Huang Yaolin to fully represent the company in handling all matters related to the aforementioned lawsuit. On May 18 of the same year, a board meeting attended by Huang Guangming and Huang Yaolin passed a resolution authorizing Huang Guangming to sign the Civil Complaint regarding the Shanghai Green Valley Company project dispute on behalf of Hong Kong Green Valley Company. On the same day, Hong Kong Green Valley Company filed a lawsuit with the Shanghai High People's Court against Xinda Company, Canada Yingming Company, Canada Green Valley Company, and Hao Xiaoying, alleging that Canada Green Valley Company had usurped Hong Kong Green Valley Company's 55% equity interest in Shanghai Green Valley Company; that Xinda Company and Canada Yingming Company, as investors, had failed to timely prevent the usurpation by Canada Green Valley Company and Hao Xiaoying, thereby infringing upon its legitimate rights and interests, and should bear corresponding liability; and that Shanghai Green Valley Company's annual after-tax profits for 1994 through 1997 were RMB 2.45 million, RMB 22.87 million, and RMB 54.13 million respectively, yet Hong Kong Green Valley Company had never received the profits distributable based on its 55% shareholding. The plaintiff requested the court to: 1. order the defendants to cease the infringement of its investment of US$5.5 million; 2. order the defendants to immediately apply to the industrial and commercial authorities to change the registration and restore its 55% equity interest, i.e., US$5.5 million, in Shanghai Green Valley Company; 3. order the defendants to pay the profits Hong Kong Green Valley Company should have received from Shanghai Green Valley Company's operations for the years 1994 to 1997; and 4. order the defendants to bear the litigation costs. During the trial, on July 13, 1999, Hong Kong Green Valley Company requested to withdraw the third claim, "order the defendants to pay the profits Hong Kong Green Valley Company should have received from Shanghai Green Valley Company's operations for the years 1994 to 1997." On October 20 of the same year, Hong Kong Green Valley Company, on the grounds that Canada Yingming Company "was completely unaware of the change of the third-party investor of Shanghai Green Valley Company from Hong Kong Green Valley Company to Canada Green Valley Company in 1995" and had reached an understanding with Canada Yingming Company, applied to withdraw the lawsuit against Canada Yingming Company. The court of first instance orally ruled to permit Hong Kong Green Valley Company to withdraw the above two claims.

On September 9, 1999, a statement notarized by the Consulate General of the People's Republic of China in Vancouver, signed by Zhao Jingjing and by Zhao Jingjing on behalf of Hao Xiaoying and Lu Jiadong, stated: Hao Xiaoying, Lu Jiadong, and Zhao Jingjing are directors of Hong Kong Green Valley Company. The board of directors had never studied or passed any resolution to file a lawsuit in the Shanghai High People's Court. They were unaware of the so-called complaint. A lawsuit initiated without the knowledge or consent of half of the directors was illegal. On March 1, 2000, a board meeting of Hong Kong Green Valley Company attended by Hao Xiaoying, Lu Jiadong, and Zhao Jingjing passed a resolution: The lawsuit filed by directors such as Huang Guangming against Xinda Company, Canada Yingming Company, Canada Green Valley Company, and Hao Xiaoying in the Shanghai High People's Court, without discussion and resolution by all directors, was invalid. It was decided to apply for withdrawal of the lawsuit in the name of Hong Kong Green Valley Company. On the same day, a "Withdrawal Application" bearing the official seal of Hong Kong Green Valley Company was sent to the Shanghai High People's Court, applying for withdrawal of the lawsuit.

On April 3, 2000, a board meeting of Hong Kong Green Valley Company attended by Huang Guangming, Huang Yaolin, and Liu Xinran passed a resolution: 1. The legal action against Canada Green Valley Company and Hao Xiaoying was lawfully taken by directors Huang Guangming, Liu Xinran, Huang Yaolin, and others, and Hao Xiaoying and others have no right to overturn it; 2. The above resolution was confirmed and adopted at an extraordinary general meeting held on May 2, 1998, attended by shareholders holding 60% of the issued shares, in order to protect the fundamental interests of the shareholders, and thus Hao Xiaoying and other directors have no right to overturn or oppose it; 3. Authorize Huang Guangming to issue a statement on behalf of the company.

On November 8, 2001, Hao Xiaoying and Lu Jiadong filed a lawsuit in the Court of First Instance of the High Court of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region against Huang Guangming, Huang Yaolin, Liu Xinran, and Hong Kong Green Valley Company, seeking a declaration on the validity of the extraordinary general meeting of Hong Kong Green Valley Company held on May 2, 1998. On August 21, 2002, the Court of First Instance of the High Court of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region rendered judgment No. 2001/5905, holding that the plaintiffs were entitled to receive notice of the extraordinary general meeting and that such notice was not validly served on the plaintiffs, but because it did not constitute fraud on the minority and the resolution was for the benefit of the company, the general meeting was ultimately held to be valid. On September 30 of the same year, the Court of Appeal of the High Court of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region docketed Case No. 2002/343, accepting the appeal filed by Hao Xiaoying and Lu Jiadong against the above judgment. That appeal is currently pending.

Additionally: Hong Kong Kaiyi Company was registered in Hong Kong under the Companies Ordinance on September 25, 1987. Its current directors are Huang Yaolin, Huang Guangming, and Liu Jianguo.

Hong Kong Green Valley Company was registered in Hong Kong under the Companies Ordinance on July 18, 1991. Its original shareholders and directors were Huang Yaolin and Liu Jianguo. On April 6, 1992, the shareholders were changed to Huang Yaolin, Huang Guangming, Liu Jianguo, Hao Xiaoying, and Lu Jiadong. In 1996, Liu Jianguo transferred his shares to Liu Xinran, and the shareholders of the company were accordingly changed to Huang Yaolin, Huang Guangming, Liu Xinran, Hao Xiaoying, and Lu Jiadong, with directors being Huang Yaolin, Huang Guangming, Liu Xinran, Hao Xiaoying, Lu Jiadong, and Zhao Jingjing. The current directors are Huang Yaolin, Huang Guangming, and Liu Xinran.

Green Valley Management Company was registered in Hong Kong under the Companies Ordinance on March 24, 1992. Its original directors were Huang Yaolin and Liu Jianguo. On April 22 of the same year, Huang Yaolin and Liu Jianguo transferred their shares to Hao Xiaoying and Lu Jiadong respectively, and the directors of the company were changed to Hao Xiaoying and Lu Jiadong. The company was subsequently dissolved.

Canada Green Valley Company was registered in Canada on June 1, 1994. Its directors are Hao Xiaoying and Lu Jiadong.

Canada Yingming Company was established in Canada on September 29, 1980. Shi Meixuan is a director of the company.

Hao Xiaoying, Lu Jiadong, Liu Jianguo, and Zhao Jingjing were directors appointed by Hong Kong Green Valley Company to Shanghai Green Valley Company. The current chairman of the board of Shanghai Green Valley Company is Hao Xiaoying, with Lu Jiadong as general manager.

The court of first instance held that: Prior to September 16, 1995, the investors of Shanghai Green Valley Company consisted of three parties: Xinda Company, Canada Yingming Company, and Hong Kong Green Valley Company, with the Chinese party contributing US$2 million, Canada Yingming Company contributing US$2.5 million, and Hong Kong Green Valley Company contributing US$5.5 million. As to whether Hong Kong Green Valley Company was renamed Canada Green Valley Company and relocated to Canada after September 16, the existing evidence fully proves that Hong Kong Green Valley Company was never renamed Canada Green Valley Company, nor did it relocate to Canada. Legally, there is no issue of renaming or relocation between companies of different nationalities. Hong Kong Green Valley Company has been operating in Hong Kong since its establishment on July 18, 1991, a fact also acknowledged by Canada Green Valley Company. Even if there were internal rights disputes among the shareholders of Hong Kong Green Valley Company, Canada Green Valley Company's acquisition of the status of a shareholder in Shanghai Green Valley Company by the aforementioned means had no factual basis and violated legal provisions, thereby infringing upon the rights and interests of Hong Kong Green Valley Company. The general meeting of shareholders is the company's authority, and the board of directors is the company's business management body. According to the existing evidence, the lawsuit filed by Hong Kong Green Valley Company was approved by three shareholders holding 60% of the equity and conformed to the company's articles of association, and thus should be valid. The withdrawal application submitted by Canada Green Valley Company in the name of Hong Kong Green Valley Company was not approved by a majority of the shareholders of Hong Kong Green Valley Company, and therefore the withdrawal application was not accepted. Canada Green Valley Company argued that Hong Kong Green Valley Company's claim was time-barred, but failed to provide evidence showing when Hong Kong Green Valley Company became aware of the infringement of its rights. The statute of limitations must be calculated from the date when the party knew or should have known that its rights were infringed. Since Hong Kong Green Valley Company authorized Hao Xiaoying to engage in business operations in Shanghai Green Valley Company, and changes in the investment entity of a foreign-invested enterprise do not require public announcement, it was possible that Hong Kong Green Valley Company was unaware of the infringement of its rights. Canada Green Valley Company's defense was difficult to sustain. As to whether the case should be accepted by the economic division or the civil division, that is a matter of internal division of labor within the court and does not affect the exercise of the parties' rights. As to whether the case should be resolved through administrative channels, since the plaintiff's claims were for confirmation of rights and cessation of infringement, and the court was to examine whether the plaintiff was the holder of rights and whether the rights were infringed, the court could certainly confirm the rights between equal civil subjects. Therefore, the court could legally determine the facts and render a judgment. Canada Green Valley Company's defense was not valid. Both Hong Kong Green Valley Company and Canada Green Valley Company and Hao Xiaoying had no dispute over the fact that the original shareholder Hong Kong Kaiyi Company in Shanghai Green Valley Company was changed to Hong Kong Green Valley Company. Therefore, Hong Kong Green Valley Company was a shareholder of Shanghai Green Valley Company and, of course, the owner of the corresponding equity. Whether it paid the capital to Hong Kong Kaiyi Company was a legal relationship between it and Hong Kong Kaiyi Company and was irrelevant to this case. Canada Green Valley Company's assertion that it was the actual capital contributor lacked supporting evidence and was not accepted. The actions taken by Hao Xiaoying, as the chairman of Canada Green Valley Company, represented the company, and the company should bear the corresponding legal liabilities according to law. Therefore, Hao Xiaoying's defense that he should not bear personal legal liability had legal basis and could be supported. As for Xinda Company, the law did not impose on it a duty to supervise and manage this matter. Xinda Company was not at fault, and Hong Kong Green Valley Company's request that Xinda Company jointly bear liability had no legal basis and was not supported. Based on the facts found, the lawsuit filed by Hong Kong Green Valley Company was valid. Canada Green Valley Company and Hao Xiaoying's argument that the case should await the judgment of the Hong Kong court before being handled was not well-founded and was not accepted. After deliberation by the judicial committee, the court, in accordance with Article 5, Article 106(2), and Article 134(1)(1) and (4) of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered the following judgment: 1. Confirmed that Hong Kong Green Valley Company is one of the shareholders of Shanghai Green Valley Company, with a total investment of US$5.5 million; 2. Canada Green Valley Company shall cease the infringement and, within ten days from the effective date of this judgment, complete the corresponding industrial and commercial registration change procedures to confirm the investment entity and the ownership of the investment as belonging to Hong Kong Green Valley Company; 3. The remaining claims of Hong Kong Green Valley Company are not supported. The case acceptance fee was RMB 237,701.75, to be borne by Canada Green Valley Company.

Canada Green Valley Company refused to accept the above judgment and appealed, claiming: 1. The original judgment ignored the basic fact that the disputed equity in this case was legally transferred, and denied that Canada Green Valley Company enjoyed the disputed equity on the grounds of defects in the procedural formalities of the equity change process, which lacked factual basis. On December 8, 1992, Hong Kong Green Valley Company borrowed money from Canada Green Valley Company due to financial constraints, and the two parties reached an agreement: Hong Kong Green Valley Company borrowed USD 5.5 million from Canada Green Valley Company for Hong Kong Green Valley Company's investment projects in Mainland China; from the date of borrowing, Hong Kong Green Valley Company would settle the principal and interest of USD 5.5 million with Canada Green Valley Company; interest was calculated at an annual rate of 10.5%, settled semi-annually, and the principal was due for lump sum repayment after two years; if it could not be repaid upon maturity, Hong Kong Green Valley Company would transfer all project shares to Canada Green Valley Company's name. The equity in the Mainland investment projects referred to in this agreement was the disputed 55% equity in Shanghai Green Valley Company in this case. After Canada Green Valley Company paid the funds according to the agreement (actually paying USD 5.7 million), and after repeated demands, Hong Kong Green Valley Company was unable to repay. Upon expiration of the loan term, Canada Green Valley Company obtained the disputed equity in accordance with the agreement, with the cooperation of Hong Kong Green Valley Company, Shanghai Green Valley Company, and other shareholders. This equity change had been approved by the Changning District People's Government of Shanghai and the industrial and commercial registration had been changed. Therefore, Canada Green Valley Company's acquisition of the 55% equity of Hong Kong Green Valley Company in Shanghai Green Valley Company was not an infringement, but the result of an equity transfer between the two parties based on the agreement. Of course, when the two parties carried out the equity transfer, in order to simplify procedures, they applied to the relevant management authorities for shareholder changes on the grounds that Hong Kong Green Valley Company had relocated and changed its name, and handled the relevant procedures, which violated relevant regulations on the management and registration of foreign-funded enterprises. However, this formal error could not necessarily change the true intent of the equity transfer between the two parties. In this regard, the parties in this case should be required to explain the situation to the relevant administrative authorities in accordance with relevant regulations and correct the relevant registration items based on the true circumstances. 2. The disputed equity change registration in this case occurred between September and November 1995, while Hong Kong Green Valley Company filed the lawsuit in May 1998. When Hong Kong Green Valley Company filed the lawsuit, it exceeded the two-year statute of limitations period stipulated in the General Principles of the Civil Law and had lost its right to win the case. The people's court should have lawfully rejected Hong Kong Green Valley Company's claims. The equity transfer was the result of an agreement between the two parties, and the board of directors of Shanghai Green Valley Company had specially convened a board meeting on the change of Party C of the company from Hong Kong Green Valley Company to Canada Green Valley Company. Representatives of Hong Kong Green Valley Company also attended that board meeting, so Hong Kong Green Valley Company was clearly aware of this change. Starting from 1994, Hong Kong Green Valley Company had not received any dividend profits from Shanghai Green Valley Company but had never made inquiries or raised objections. It only claimed distribution of profits after 1994 at the time of litigation. This also shows that Hong Kong Green Valley Company not only knew that its equity had been transferred to Canada Green Valley Company but also had no objection to the transfer. Therefore, the statute of limitations in this case should be calculated from September 1995, or at the latest from November 1995. Hong Kong Green Valley Company did not provide any evidence to prove when it became aware that its equity had been changed. The original judgment found, on the grounds that there was a possibility that Hong Kong Green Valley Company was unaware of the infringement of its rights, that its lawsuit did not exceed the statute of limitations and ruled in its favor, which was clearly erroneous. 3. In the equity change registration activities involved in this case, Shanghai Green Valley Company was not only a participant but also the implementer of the specific work. Moreover, whether its major shareholder was Hong Kong Green Valley Company or Canada Green Valley Company would have a significant impact on the company's operation and development. Therefore, whether from the perspective of whether there was joint infringement, or from the perspective of facilitating the ascertainment of the facts of the case, or from the perspective of the impact of the judgment result, Shanghai Green Valley Company should have been a necessary party to participate in this litigation. Although Hong Kong Green Valley Company did not list Shanghai Green Valley Company as a defendant when filing the lawsuit, the court of first instance should have lawfully added Shanghai Green Valley Company as a defendant in this case. The failure to list the party by the court of first instance not only affected the determination of the facts of this case but also violated the relevant provisions of the Civil Procedure Law and should be corrected. 4. The court of first instance lightly accepted the case without seriously examining Hong Kong Green Valley Company's lawsuit filing and, during the trial, refused to wait for the outcome of another case that might have ruled that Hong Kong Green Valley Company's lawsuit was invalid, violating the relevant provisions of the Civil Procedure Law. According to the Hong Kong Companies Ordinance, a company's litigation action must be supported by shareholders holding 95% of the company's shares before it can be initiated. When examining a lawsuit, the people's court should carefully verify the company's shareholders' meeting resolution to ensure that the lawsuit filing is valid; otherwise, erroneous case acceptance may occur. In this case, when Hong Kong Green Valley Company filed the lawsuit, there was only a board resolution attended by two directors, and no shareholders' meeting resolution. The court of first instance not only failed to verify whether Hong Kong Green Valley Company's lawsuit filing complied with relevant provisions when accepting the case but also groundlessly found that "according to the existing evidence, Hong Kong Green Valley Company's lawsuit filing was approved by three shareholders holding 60% of the company's equity, complied with the company's articles of association, and should be valid." During the trial of this case, other shareholders of Hong Kong Green Valley Company believed that the lawsuit filing violated the company's articles of association and the relevant provisions of the Hong Kong Companies Ordinance. They had filed a lawsuit with the Hong Kong court, requesting a declaration that the lawsuit filed in the court of first instance in the name of Hong Kong Green Valley Company was invalid. The Hong Kong court was still hearing that case. Canada Green Valley Company notified the court of first instance of the relevant circumstances and applied in court for a stay of the proceedings in this case, pending the outcome of the Hong Kong court's trial. The court of first instance did not lawfully rule to stay the proceedings in this case but continued the trial and issued a judgment, which was clearly erroneous. 5. Hong Kong Green Valley Company had submitted a written application for withdrawal of the lawsuit. The court of first instance continued the trial without issuing any ruling, violating the relevant provisions of the Civil Procedure Law. On March 1, 2000, other shareholders of Hong Kong Green Valley Company also submitted a "Withdrawal of Claim Application" to the court of first instance in the name of Hong Kong Green Valley Company, bearing the company seal, requesting withdrawal of the claim. After receiving the withdrawal application, the court of first instance did not issue a ruling but instead handled it in the judgment by rejecting Canada Green Valley Company's defense, erroneously treating the withdrawal application submitted by other shareholders of Hong Kong Green Valley Company in the name of Hong Kong Green Valley Company as a withdrawal application submitted by Canada Green Valley Company in the name of Hong Kong Green Valley Company. In summary, the original judgment had serious errors in fact-finding, law application, and trial procedure. Therefore, it requested: to set aside the original judgment, confirm that Canada Green Valley Company is one of the shareholders of Shanghai Green Valley Company, with a total investment of USD 5.5 million, representing 55% equity; or order a remand of the case to the court of first instance for retrial.

The appellee Hong Kong Green Valley Company argued in its defense: 1. Canada Green Valley Company claims that the disputed equity in the case was legally transferred, while at the same time admitting defects in the procedural formalities of the equity change process, which is contradictory. Canada Green Valley Company claims that it reached a loan agreement with Hong Kong Green Valley Company on December 8, 1992, but the establishment date of Canada Green Valley Company was June 1, 1994. At the time the agreement was reached, the legal personality of Canada Green Valley Company did not yet exist, and it did not produce the formal document of that agreement to the court, so the agreement does not exist. Hong Kong Green Valley Company never borrowed money from Canada Green Valley Company. The so-called remittance slips produced by Canada Green Valley Company were economic transactions between a third party, Green Valley Management Company, Zhao Jingying, and Hao Xiaoying, and others, and were not loan vouchers, nor equity transfer payments, nor registration certificates. They merely indicated the destination of Zhao Jingying's private funds. Zhao Jingying is Hao Xiaoying's wife, and her testimony has no evidentiary validity whatsoever. Some of the evidence it produced were documents without dates and with no legal effect, others were perjured evidence provided in court, and all involved third parties, having no connection whatsoever to the infringement facts involved in this case. Therefore, Canada Green Valley Company is not a lawful investor in Shanghai Green Valley Company. 2. Canada Green Valley Company falsely reported that "the investor of Party C of Shanghai Green Valley Company was Hong Kong Green Valley Company, and because the company relocated to Canada and was registered in Canada, the original Hong Kong Green Valley Company was renamed Canada Green Valley Company, with the legal representative and chairman unchanged, and the equity of the investor of Party C of Shanghai Green Valley Company remained unchanged." At that time, Shanghai Green Valley Company had three shareholders, one of which was Hong Kong Green Valley Company, another was Canada Yingming Company. The chairman of that company, Shi Meixuan, declared on September 15, 1998, that "regarding the change of Party C Hong Kong Green Valley Company to Canada Green Valley Company in 1995, Party B was completely unaware," and on March 4, 2002, again issued a notarized declaration reiterating that it was unaware of the shareholder change matter. Another shareholder, Xinda Company, also stated that it was unclear about the above disputed facts. Canada Green Valley Company deceived the superior authority, the Changning District People's Government of Shanghai, and obtained the approval document "agreeing that the original investor Party C, Hong Kong Green Valley Company, because it changed its registration to Canada, be changed to Canada Green Valley Company," and deceived the Shanghai Administration for Industry and Commerce, changing the industrial and commercial registration. By doing so, Canada Green Valley Company intended to show its legality, concealing its means and essence of encroachment. The director at the time of the change registration, Mr. Liu Jianguo, declared: "I, Liu Jianguo, was a director of Shanghai Green Valley Company (as recorded in the Shanghai industrial and commercial change registration items on November 23, 1995). In that registration form, the investor Hong Kong Green Valley Company had been changed to Canada Green Valley Company. I declare that I was unaware of this change both before and after it occurred. At the same time, during the period from 1995 to 1998, I met with Mr. Huang Guangming and Mr. Huang Yaolin on several occasions, and they never mentioned anything about the change of equity, because they, like me, did not know that Hong Kong Green Valley Company's equity in Shanghai Green Valley Company had been changed to Canada Green Valley Company." 3. Hong Kong Green Valley Company and Canada Green Valley Company are the parties concerning the disputed equity in this case, while Shanghai Green Valley Company is merely a community formed by the three investors' joint participation and has nothing to do with the equity dispute. There is no equity dispute issue between the investors. Canada Green Valley Company's request to add Shanghai Green Valley Company as a party to this case has no legal basis. Moreover, according to the Civil Procedure Law of China, a plaintiff may waive or modify its claims and has the right to dispose of its rights in accordance with the law. 4. Canada Green Valley Company argues that this case should be governed by Hong Kong law and requests that the Mainland court stay the trial of this case because it has filed a lawsuit in the Hong Kong court, which has no legal basis. Moreover, the Hong Kong court had already dismissed its original claim on August 21, 2002. Hong Kong Green Valley Company, based on the actions of Hao Xiaoying and Lyu Jiadong that harmed its interests, called a special general meeting before filing the lawsuit, and only filed the lawsuit after obtaining the approval of 60% of the shareholders at the special general meeting. Canada Green Valley Company also applied for withdrawal of the claim in the name of Hong Kong Green Valley Company. On April 3, 2000, Hong Kong Green Valley Company again passed a resolution at a special general meeting with 60% of shareholders that "Canada Green Valley Company has no right to make any resolutions on behalf of Hong Kong Green Valley Company." According to Mainland law, the general meeting of shareholders is the company's authority organ, and the board of directors is the company's business management organ. Hong Kong Green Valley Company's lawsuit filing, having been approved by shareholders holding 60% of the company's equity, complies with the company's articles of association and is lawful and valid. The court of first instance was correct in not accepting the withdrawal application submitted by Canada Green Valley Company. In summary, the original judgment had clear facts, correct application of law, and lawful trial procedures. Therefore, it requests that the appeal be dismissed and the original judgment affirmed.

This Court holds: The essence of the dispute in this case is the controversy between Hong Kong Green Valley Company and Canada Green Valley Company over the ownership of the 55% equity in Shanghai Green Valley Company. The focus of the dispute between the two parties is: Hong Kong Green Valley Company claims that Canada Green Valley Company falsely reported that "the investor of Party C of Shanghai Green Valley Company was Hong Kong Green Valley Company, and because the company relocated to Canada and was registered in Canada, the original Hong Kong Green Valley Company was renamed Canada Green Valley Company." The Changning District People's Government of Shanghai approved that "the original investor Party C, Hong Kong Green Valley Company, because it changed its registration to Canada, be changed to Canada Green Valley Company," and the corresponding industrial and commercial registration also changed "Hong Kong Green Valley Company" to "Canada Green Valley Company," making Canada Green Valley Company the investor in Shanghai Green Valley Company, holding 55% equity. Since Hong Kong Green Valley Company could not have relocated to Canada, it is still the owner of the 55% equity in Shanghai Green Valley Company. Therefore, it filed a lawsuit with the people's court requesting an order that Canada Green Valley Company cease the infringement and apply to the industrial and commercial authorities for a change of registration to return its 55% equity (i.e., USD 5.5 million) in Shanghai Green Valley Company. In contrast, Canada Green Valley Company argues that Green Valley Management Company was the fundraiser of the USD 5.5 million, and based on the "equity mortgage agreement" with Hong Kong Green Valley Company, it exercised the "mortgage right" when Hong Kong Green Valley Company failed to repay the USD 5.5 million, obtained the 55% equity in Shanghai Green Valley Company, and transferred that equity to Canada Green Valley Company. Therefore, Canada Green Valley Company lawfully obtained the 55% equity in Shanghai Green Valley Company, and the reason given when handling the change procedures—that Hong Kong Green Valley Company had "relocated to Canada"—was to simplify procedures. Moreover, when Hong Kong Green Valley Company had previously obtained the 55% equity in Shanghai Green Valley Company from Hong Kong Kaiyi Company, it had also done so on the grounds that Hong Kong Kaiyi Company had been "renamed Hong Kong Green Valley Company." Whether Canada Green Valley Company lawfully enjoys the 55% equity in Shanghai Green Valley Company is the specific issue to be resolved in this case.

However, from the grounds of appeal and defense of the parties in this case, there is also a dispute between the parties as to who can represent Hong Kong Green Valley Company to initiate this litigation, i.e., whether the lawsuit filed by Hong Kong Green Valley Company in this case is lawful. This should be the first issue to be resolved in this case.

Hong Kong Green Valley Company is a limited liability company established under the Companies Ordinance in Hong Kong. Hao Xiaoying, Lyu Jiadong, Huang Yaolin, Huang Guangming, and Liu Xinran are each shareholders holding 20% of the company's shares. Can Huang Yaolin, Huang Guangming, and Liu Xinran initiate this litigation through a so-called "special general meeting" resolution? This involves the issue of a legal person's capacity for civil conduct. By reference to Article 184 of the Supreme People's Court's Opinions on Several Issues Concerning the Implementation of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China (Trial Implementation), "the capacity for civil conduct of a legal person is determined by its national law" and "for a foreign legal person, the law of the country where it is registered and domiciled is its national law." Therefore, in this case, it should be determined based on Hong Kong law whether the three shareholders holding 60% of the company's shares, Huang Yaolin, Huang Guangming, and Liu Xinran, could, without the participation of Hao Xiaoying and Lyu Jiadong, pass a shareholders' meeting resolution to represent Hong Kong Green Valley Company in filing the lawsuit. According to the provisions of Hong Kong company law, resolutions on major company matters, the convening of shareholders' meetings or special general meetings, etc., should be conducted in accordance with the company's articles of association. In this case, the special general meeting attended by Huang Yaolin and Huang Guangming resolved to initiate this litigation, with Huang Yaolin also representing Liu Xinran. That is, shareholders holding 60% of the company's shares and a majority of more than 60% attended the special general meeting and passed the resolution to initiate this litigation. According to the provisions of Hong Kong Green Valley Company's articles of association, all shareholders should receive notice of such meetings. Hao Xiaoying and Lyu Jiadong did not receive effective notice of that meeting, thus violating the company's articles of association. However, the special general meeting resolution of May 12, 1998, was to protect the interests of Hong Kong Green Valley Company and did not constitute fraud against the minority shareholders, Hao Xiaoying and Lyu Jiadong. Although it was contrary to the interests of Hao Xiaoying and Lyu Jiadong, according to the principles established in Hong Kong case law, the special general meeting should be deemed valid. Therefore, the lawsuit initiated pursuant to the special general meeting resolution of Hong Kong Green Valley Company on May 12, 1998, is valid. Consequently, the board resolution of Hong Kong Green Valley Company attended by Hao Xiaoying, Lyu Jiadong, and Zhao Jingying on March 1, 2000, purporting to withdraw this lawsuit in the name of Hong Kong Green Valley Company, is invalid. The appellant's arguments regarding the issue of standing to sue in this case cannot be sustained and should not be supported.

This case involves foreign-related and Hong Kong-related matters. According to the general norms of conflict of laws, procedural issues shall be governed by the law of the forum. Therefore, the procedural issues in this case shall be governed by the law of Mainland China. This case is an action for confirmation of rights. Generally speaking, disputes over confirmation of rights can be resolved through civil litigation. However, the "confirmation of rights" in this case has its special features, namely, it involves the change of equity in a sino-foreign equity joint venture enterprise. Shanghai Green Valley Company is a sino-foreign equity joint venture enterprise. According to the laws of China on sino-foreign equity joint ventures, the establishment, change, and termination of such enterprises must be submitted to the relevant competent authorities for examination and approval, and the corresponding registration procedures with the industrial and commercial authorities must be completed before they become effective. With respect to the change of equity in a sino-foreign equity joint venture enterprise, the approval of the relevant administrative department constitutes a substantive element, not a procedural or formal requirement. A change without approval is naturally void. In this case, the 55% equity of Canada Green Valley Company in Shanghai Green Valley Company had been approved by the relevant competent authority, and the corresponding registration procedures had been completed, meeting the valid legal requirements. Now, Hong Kong Green Valley Company claims that the 55% equity in Shanghai Green Valley Company should belong to it, arguing that the change of Hong Kong Green Valley Company's 55% equity in Shanghai Green Valley Company to Canada Green Valley Company was improper. Although Hong Kong Green Valley Company filed a civil lawsuit with the people's court, naming Canada Green Valley Company as the defendant and citing an equity dispute, the essence of the matter is to negate the approval of the Changning District People's Government of Shanghai, the registration of the Shanghai Administration for Industry and Commerce, and the Certificate of Approval for Foreign-Invested Enterprise issued by the Shanghai Municipal Government—i.e., to negate the specific administrative acts of the relevant administrative departments. Generally, courts can, through the result of a civil judgment, directly or indirectly cause changes to certain administrative acts, but these administrative acts should be understood as merely procedural or formal acts, such as record-filing or registration. For substantive administrative acts, such as the approval act in this case, it is a unique power granted by Chinese law to the relevant administrative departments and cannot be changed through civil litigation proceedings or civil judgments. Even if the approval is improper, it can only be corrected through administrative reconsideration proceedings or administrative litigation proceedings. Therefore, Hong Kong Green Valley Company's claim in this case for confirmation of its equity in a sino-foreign equity joint venture enterprise can only be resolved through administrative reconsideration or administrative litigation, not through the civil litigation in this case. Article 111 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "With respect to the following lawsuits, they shall be handled respectively: (1) Where, according to the provisions of the Administrative Procedure Law, a case falls within the scope of acceptance of administrative cases, the plaintiff shall be informed to file an administrative lawsuit." In this case, Hong Kong Green Valley Company should have been informed to file an administrative lawsuit. The court of first instance's issuance of a civil judgment directly changing a specific administrative act through civil litigation proceedings was improper and should be corrected. Hong Kong Green Valley Company's filing of this civil lawsuit was improper, and its claim should be dismissed.

In summary, this Court, pursuant to Article 111 of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC and Article 186 of the Opinions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues concerning the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, rules as follows:

1. Civil Judgment No. 10 (1998) of the Shanghai High People's Court is set aside;

2. The lawsuit filed by Lügu Investment Co., Ltd. is dismissed.

Court acceptance fees for the first and second instances, each in the amount of RMB 237,701.75, shall be borne by Lügu Investment Co., Ltd.

This ruling is final.
